questions.question: What does the generalized Extreme Value Theorem guarantee for a continuous function $f\colon \boldsymbol{E}\to \mathbb{R}$ on a compact set $\boldsymbol{X}\subseteq \boldsymbol{E}$?
options: It attains both a maximum and a minimum on $\boldsymbol{X}$.
It is constant on $\boldsymbol{X}$.
It is differentiable at every point of $\boldsymbol{X}$.
It maps $\boldsymbol{X}$ onto all of $\mathbb{R}$.
questions.explanation: The generalized EVT states that a continuous real-valued function on a compact set $\boldsymbol{X}$ attains both its maximum and its minimum on $\boldsymbol{X}$.
questions.source_support: The theorem states that a continuous real-valued function on a compact set attains both its maximum and minimum.
option_explanations: The function need not be constant; $f(x)=x$ on $[0,1]$ is continuous and non-constant, yet attains its max $1$ and min $0$.
Continuity does not imply differentiability; $f(x)=|x|$ on $[-1,1]$ is continuous but not differentiable at $0$, and the theorem needs only continuity.
The image of a compact set under a continuous function is compact, hence bounded; $f(x)=x$ on $[0,1]$ has image $[0,1]$, not all of $\mathbb{R}$.

questions.question: What does the phrase 'attains its maximum' mean here?
options: There is some $\boldsymbol{x}\in\boldsymbol{X}$ such that $f(\boldsymbol{x})$ is the largest value of $f$ on $\boldsymbol{X}$.
The values of $f$ get arbitrarily large near $\boldsymbol{X}$.
The formula for $f$ contains a largest coefficient.
The set $\boldsymbol{X}$ has largest dimension.
questions.explanation: Attaining a maximum means there exists x in X where f(x) is the largest value of f on X.
questions.source_support: The interpretation says the function must actually hit both a maximum and a minimum somewhere inside the set.
option_explanations: Arbitrarily large is not attained.

Attainment is a property of the values of $f$ on $\boldsymbol X$: there exists $\boldsymbol{x}\in\boldsymbol X$ with $f(\boldsymbol{x})=\sup_{\boldsymbol X}f$, whereas coefficients are syntactic features of one chosen formula and can change under rewriting (e.g. $x^2$ vs $2x\cdot\tfrac12 x$) without changing the attained maximum.

The maximum is taken over the values $f(\boldsymbol{x})$ for $\boldsymbol{x}\in\boldsymbol X$, a property of the function range, while the dimension $n$ of the ambient $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a fixed integer of the domain and is not a quantity of which $\boldsymbol X$ has a largest instance.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

questions.question: Which statement is a safe use of the generalized Extreme Value Theorem in optimisation?
options: If the feasible set is open, every continuous objective has an optimal maximum.
If the objective is discontinuous, compactness alone guarantees an optimum.
If the feasible set is compact and the objective is continuous, an optimal maximum and minimum exist.
If the objective is continuous, no condition on the feasible set is needed.
questions.explanation: The generalized EVT needs both hypotheses together: a compact feasible set and a continuous objective. Compactness stops the optimum from escaping to a limiting value that is never reached, and continuity ensures the objective actually attains its supremum and infimum; with both, a maximum and a minimum exist.
questions.source_support: The relevant results mention optimisation and the theorem's compactness and continuity assumptions.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).
option_explanations: An open feasible set lets the optimum escape; $f(x)=x$ on $(0,1)$ is continuous but attains neither a maximum nor a minimum.
Continuity is essential; a discontinuous objective on a compact set can fail to attain its supremum, e.g. $f(x)=x$ on $[0,1)$ with $f(1)=0$ has supremum $1$ but no maximum.
Continuity alone is insufficient without compactness; $f(x)=x$ on the open interval $(0,1)$ is continuous but attains no extreme values.
